conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You were admitted last night after coming to the ER with nausea, vomiting, and some back pain. How are you feeling now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not great. I’ve been sick all night. I drank orange juice after I got home yesterday and it made me vomit right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. That sounds like your gastroparesis acting up again. We’re keeping you on bowel rest for now—no food or drink by mouth—so your stomach can settle.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’m so hungry. How long will I have to go without eating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start small once the vomiting stops. For now, we’re giving you fluids and medications through your IV to keep you hydrated and control nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My back hurts too. Can I get something for that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re managing your pain with IV medications. But we’re being careful because some painkillers can worsen nausea or constipation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just feel so overwhelmed. I’m tired of being sick all the time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. It’s a lot to manage. We’ve asked Psychiatry to see you to help talk through some of this. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs show your blood sugar was 146 when you arrived—good, no ketoacidosis. But your creatinine is up to 1.6, which means your kidneys aren’t filtering well right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My kidneys were bad before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s acute kidney injury, likely from dehydration. We’re giving you IV fluids to help. It should improve as you stabilize.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also found a urinary tract infection. Your urine test showed bacteria, and the culture grew coagulase-negative staph.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t even feel like I had a UTI. Shouldn’t I have burning or something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not always. With diabetes, infections can be silent. We’re treating it with antibiotics—started on Cipro, now switching to Macrobid to finish the course.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve had some diarrhea too. We think this could be gastroenteritis on top of your gastroparesis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not just my diabetes acting up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s both. The infection and vomiting are making it harder for your stomach to empty, which is why we’re keeping you NPO for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high—149/100 earlier. We gave IV metoprolol since you’re not eating. Once you can take pills, we’ll restart lisinopril.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I forgot to take it before I came in. I’ve been so stressed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. We’ll get it back on track. We’re planning to increase it to 20 mg daily to help control your BP better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your IV stopped working last night, so we’re going to place a PICC line today to make giving fluids and meds easier.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What’s a PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s a longer IV line that goes into a vein in your arm and up toward your heart. It’ll stay in for a few days to avoid needing new IVs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The PICC line was placed successfully this morning. You’re now getting fluids and antibiotics through it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels weird in my arm. Is it supposed to go all the way to my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it goes into a large vein near your heart. A chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right spot. You might see it on the monitor—it extends a bit into the right atrium, but that’s safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is coming down—from 1.6 to 1.2. That’s a good sign your kidneys are recovering with hydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I try drinking something now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll start with small sips of water. If you keep that down, we’ll advance to clear liquids tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well last night—no vomiting. We’re going to start you on a diabetic liquid diet and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have insulin with it? I don’t want my sugar to spike.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You’re back on your full dose of Lantus—24 units at bedtime—and we’ll use Humalog as a sliding scale with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Psychiatry met with you yesterday. They think your anxiety is playing a big role in how you’re coping with your health.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I just feel out of control. When I get anxious, I can’t move, I can’t think.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. Social work is helping find a new counselor for you. They also suggest restarting an SSRI to help manage the anxiety long-term.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve kept down the liquid diet. We’re going to advance you to soft foods—mashed potatoes, applesauce—still diabetic-friendly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I have Reglan with meals? It usually helps my stomach empty.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve restarted Reglan—now four times a day instead of three. That should help with gastroparesis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you’ve had no nausea or vomiting for two days. Your blood pressure is also much better on the increased lisinopril dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. We’ll make sure you can keep down solid food and that your blood sugars are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We had a family meeting with social work. We talked about how stress and anxiety might be making your physical symptoms worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t say much, but I heard you. I do want to feel better—mentally too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great step. We’ll get you set up with follow-up for both your PCP and a counselor. You’re not alone in this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. You’re eating regular food, no vomiting, and your labs are improving. We’re planning to discharge you this morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my meds? Anything changed?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. Lisinopril is now 20 mg daily, Reglan is four times a day, and you’ll continue Zofran as needed. Insulin stays the same—24 units Lantus at night and Humalog with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish the Macrobid as prescribed. Drink plenty of fluids to prevent another UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try. And I’ll call to set up that counseling appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the plan. Get your labs checked soon to make sure your kidneys and electrolytes are stable. You’re doing great.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The discharge papers are ready. You’re cleared to go home. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and don’t hesitate to call if things worsen.
